source: CPTS Module 03: Network Enumeration with Nmap

examples.label: Trace packets on a single port

notes: `--top-ports N` scans the N most common ports (from nmap-services frequency data) - fast triage, but a full `-p-` is required before declaring a host clean.

references.title: HTB Academy - Network Enumeration with Nmap

name: Nmap - Top Ports / Port Specification
description: Scan the most common ports, or specify exactly which ports to scan. Port selection is the main lever on scan scope vs speed.

defense.why_it_works: The --top-ports flag scans the most commonly open ports based on frequency data from nmap-services, making scans faster while still covering the services most likely to be running. Attackers use this to quickly identify attack surface without a full 65535-port scan. [MITRE T1046] Targeted port scanning to identify running services.
defense.impact: Fast coverage of the most commonly open services, trading completeness for speed.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1046 AN1583] Monitor for rapid sequential port connection attempts from a single source to many ports or hosts. Nmap with --top-ports generates a characteristic pattern of SYN packets across common service ports in quick succession.
defense.artifacts: SYN probes to the top-N ports in firewall/IDS logs.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1046 M1042] Close unnecessary ports and services to reduce attack surface exposed to scanning. Use host-based and network firewalls to block unsolicited inbound connections. [M1030] Segment networks to limit which hosts can be reached by a scanning adversary.
defense.evasion: Scanning only the most common ports (--top-ports) sharply cuts packet volume and scan time versus a full sweep, lowering the footprint; add slow timing (-T1) to stay under rate-based IDS thresholds.
defense.misconfiguration: Network perimeters that do not filter ICMP, do not use egress filtering, or expose unnecessary services (all ports open) allow comprehensive port scanning. Systems without host-based firewalls or IDS/IPS allow scan traffic to enumerate every open service, revealing attack surface. No rate-limiting on inbound probes means stealth scans complete quickly.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# No firewall between attacker and target (or overly permissive rules):
# iptables -L  ->  Chain INPUT (policy ACCEPT)  [no rules]
# Or: Windows Firewall disabled
# Every service's port is reachable from any source

# No IDS/IPS:
# Snort/Suricata not deployed; no AWS GuardDuty / Azure Defender
# Nmap SYN scan completes in seconds with no alert generated
defense.secure_config:
# Linux host-based firewall — default-deny inbound:
iptables -P INPUT DROP
iptables -P FORWARD DROP
iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
# Only open required services:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT  # HTTPS only
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 10.10.1.0/24 -j ACCEPT  # SSH from mgmt network

# Rate-limit scan detection (drops SYN floods):
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --syn -m limit --limit 1/s --limit-burst 3 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --syn -j DROP

# Deploy IDS/IPS:
# Snort/Suricata rules detect nmap OS detection probes
# AWS: GuardDuty (detects port scans from EC2)
# Cloud: Security Groups default-deny with explicit allow rules
